question_text: A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of gradually worsening rhythmic movements of his right hand for the past 5 months. His symptoms worsen when he is in a meeting and he is concerned that people are noticing it more frequently. There is no personal or family history of serious illness, but the patient recalls that his father developed bobbing of the head in older age. He takes no medications. Neurological examination shows a tremor of the right hand when the limbs are relaxed. When the patient is asked to move his arm the tremor decreases. He has reduced arm swing while walking. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

                    ### Question
                    A 50-year-old man comes to the physician because of gradually worsening rhythmic movements of his right hand for the past 5 months. His symptoms worsen when he is in a meeting and he is concerned that people are noticing it more frequently. There is no personal or family history of serious illness, but the patient recalls that his father developed bobbing of the head in older age. He takes no medications. Neurological examination shows a tremor of the right hand when the limbs are relaxed. When the patient is asked to move his arm the tremor decreases. He has reduced arm swing while walking. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacotherapy?

                    ### Options
                    opa. Donepezil
opb. Trihexyphenidyl
opc. Clonazepam
opd. Propranolol
ope. Levodopa/carbidopa

### Enhanced Information (For Contextual Support):
The patient presents with a right hand tremor that worsens with stress and decreases with movement, which is characteristic of a resting tremor, commonly associated with Parkinson's disease. However, the family history of head bobbing suggests a hereditary movement disorder, potentially indicating essential tremor. Propranolol is a first-line treatment for essential tremor, which aligns with the consensus that beta-blockers are effective for this condition. Although Levodopa/carbidopa is a standard treatment for Parkinson's disease, the overall presentation leans more towards essential tremor, making Propranolol the most appropriate pharmacotherapy in this case.
